slides.heading:
Humanoid Robots:
The Next Frontier
slides.body: How machines that walk, talk, and work are reshaping our world in 2026

slides.heading: The Inflection Point
slides.body: 2025–2026 marks the year humanoid robots moved from research labs into real workplaces. What was science fiction a decade ago is now a global industry race worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

slides.heading: Who's Building Them
slides.body: Tesla Optimus, Figure AI, Boston Dynamics Atlas, 1X Technologies, and Agility Robotics are leading the charge. China's Unitree and Fourier Intelligence are close behind, making this a global competition.

slides.heading: How They Move
slides.body: Modern humanoids combine reinforcement learning, whole-body control algorithms, and dense sensor arrays. They learn complex motions by watching humans via imitation learning, then refine skills in simulation.

slides.heading: Real-World Deployments
slides.body: BMW's Spartanburg plant uses Figure robots on assembly lines. Amazon pilots Agility's Digit in fulfillment centers. Tesla deploys Optimus units internally for factory tasks — real work, not demos.

slides.heading: The Training Revolution
slides.body: Teleoperation lets human operators 'puppet' robots to collect training data. Paired with massive simulation environments, robots can accumulate millions of hours of virtual experience before touching the real world.

slides.heading: The Cost Barrier
slides.body: Today's humanoid units cost $50,000–$150,000 each. Manufacturers are targeting sub-$20,000 by the decade's end through mass production and commodity hardware — the same cost curve that drove smartphones.

slides.heading: Safety & Trust
slides.body: Robots operate under strict force-limiting software to prevent injury. Human oversight systems, geofencing, and emergency-stop protocols are mandatory. Building public trust is as hard as building the robots themselves.

slides.heading: The Jobs Question
slides.body: History shows automation creates new roles even as it displaces others. Humanoid robots will likely take on dangerous, repetitive, or physically demanding tasks — freeing humans for higher-value work. The transition won't be painless.

slides.heading: The Robot Decade Has Begun
slides.body: The next 10 years will define how humans and robots coexist. The question is no longer if humanoid robots will transform society — it's how fast, and whether we're ready.
